gloss: To promote something far more than it deserves, so that people expect too much.
examples: Studios *overhype* almost every summer release.
The company *overhyped* the product and buyers were disappointed.
Critics say the threat has been badly *overhyped*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*they overindulge their kids*), intransitive (*we overindulged at dinner*)
gloss: To have too much of something enjoyable, or to give someone far too much of what they want.
examples: It is easy to *overindulge* at a buffet.
We *overindulged* over the holidays and paid for it in January.
Grandparents are famous for *overindulging* their grandchildren.

gloss: To put too much air into something, or to make something seem far bigger than it is.
examples: Do not *overinflate* the tires before a long drive.
The agency *overinflated* the number of visitors.
He has an *overinflated* sense of his own importance.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the tiles overlap each other*), intransitive (*our shifts overlap*)
gloss: To cover part of something else, or to happen partly at the same time as something else.
examples: Our shifts *overlap* by an hour every Friday.
The two studies *overlapped* almost completely.
The shingles are *overlapping* so that rain runs off.
contrast: The verb stresses the last syllable, oh-vur-LAP; the noun stresses the first, OH-vur-lap. The p doubles: *overlapped*, *overlapping*.

gloss: To put more weight, work, or data on something than it can carry.
examples: Do not *overload* the washing machine.
The storm *overloaded* the power grid.
Students are *overloaded* with assignments this term.
contrast: Verb oh-vur-LOHD, noun OH-vur-lohd (*an overload of information*).

gloss: To make something seem more important or more certain than it really is.
examples: Do not *overplay* the risk; the odds are still good.
The senator *overplayed* his hand and lost the vote.
Reporters have been *overplaying* one bad poll.

gloss: To fill a place with more people or animals than it can support.
examples: Rabbits can *overpopulate* an island in a single season.
The deer *overpopulated* the park within a decade.
The lake is *overpopulated* with carp.

ru: завышать цену, назначать слишком высокую цену
gloss: To charge more for something than it is worth.
examples: Airport shops *overprice* everything.
They *overpriced* the house and it sat unsold for a year.
The wine list is wildly *overpriced*.

gloss: To protect someone so much that you keep them from normal experience.
examples: Parents who *overprotect* their children leave them unprepared.
She admits she *overprotected* her youngest son.
He grew up feeling *overprotected*.

gloss: To think someone or something is better or more important than it really is.
examples: Fans *overrate* any quarterback who wins early.
Most critics *overrated* the first album.
That restaurant is completely *overrated*.

ru: зарываться, брать на себя слишком много, переусердствовать
transitivity: both — intransitive (*the company overreached*), transitive (*he overreached himself*)
gloss: To try to do more than you can manage or have the right to do, and fail because of it.
examples: Startups often *overreach* in their second year.
The governor *overreached* and the courts struck the order down.
By *overreaching*, the union lost the gains it already had.

gloss: To react much more strongly than a situation deserves.
examples: Try not to *overreact* to one bad grade.
Management *overreacted* and fired the whole team.
He is *overreacting*, as usual.
contrast: Followed by *to*: *overreact to the news*.

ru: представлять непропорционально широко; быть чрезмерно представленным
gloss: To give a group more seats, places, or attention than its share of the population deserves.
examples: The Senate *overrepresents* small states.
Early surveys *overrepresented* homeowners.
Men are heavily *overrepresented* in the field.

gloss: To make something else seem less important or less noticed.
examples: One scandal can *overshadow* a decade of good work.
Her older brother's record *overshadowed* everything she did.
The news conference was *overshadowed* by the storm.

ru: выбалтывать лишнее, рассказывать слишком много личного
transitivity: both — intransitive (*he overshares constantly*), transitive (*she overshared the details*)
gloss: To tell people more personal detail than they want to hear.
examples: Some coworkers *overshare* the minute they sit down.
He *overshared* about his divorce at the office party.
She apologized for *oversharing* online.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the article oversimplifies the issue*), intransitive (*I am oversimplifying here*)
gloss: To explain something so simply that what is left is misleading or wrong.
examples: Textbooks *oversimplify* the causes of the war.
The summary *oversimplified* a complicated ruling.
I am *oversimplifying*, but that is the basic idea.
contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: *oversimplifies*, *oversimplified*, but *oversimplifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To describe something as larger, worse, or more certain than it really is.
examples: It is hard to *overstate* how much the city has changed.
The report *overstated* the savings by half.
The danger has been *overstated* from the beginning.

gloss: To go beyond a limit of what is allowed or acceptable.
examples: Do not *overstep* your authority on this.
The agency *overstepped* its legal powers.
He knew he was *overstepping* the moment he said it.
contrast: The p doubles: *overstepped*, *overstepping*. The old form *overstept* is not used in American English.

gloss: To put more strain on someone or something than it can stand, or to tax people too heavily.
examples: Twelve-hour shifts *overtax* the nurses.
The climb *overtaxed* his knees.
Emergency rooms are *overtaxed* every flu season.

gloss: To use something too much or too often, so that it wears out or loses its effect.
examples: Beginning writers *overuse* adverbs.
Doctors once *overused* antibiotics for ordinary colds.
The trail is badly *overused* in summer.
contrast: The verb ends in a z-sound, oh-vur-YOOZ; the noun ends in an s-sound, OH-vur-yoos.

gloss: To decide or state that something is worth more than it really is.
examples: Investors *overvalue* companies that grow fast early on.
The bank *overvalued* the property by two hundred thousand dollars.
The currency is *overvalued* against the dollar.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the firm overworks its staff*), intransitive (*he overworks every spring*)
gloss: To work too hard, or to make someone work too hard.
examples: Small clinics *overwork* their nurses.
She *overworked* all spring and got sick in May.
The crew looks *overworked* and underpaid.
contrast: The past is *overworked*; *overwrought* is a different word, meaning very upset.

gloss: To release an egg from the ovary.
examples: Most women *ovulate* about two weeks before a period.
She *ovulated* late that month, which threw off the calculation.
The app tracks the days she is *ovulating*.

gloss: To add soft material to something to make it softer, thicker, or better protected.
examples: They *pad* the walls of the studio to deaden the sound.
She *padded* the box with newspaper before shipping it.
The jacket is *padded* at the shoulders.
contrast: The d doubles: *padded*, *padding*. The same verb also means to add unnecessary extra, as in *pad an expense report*.

gloss: To fasten or close something with a padlock.
examples: Crews *padlock* the gate at dusk.
The city *padlocked* the restaurant after two failed inspections.
Our bikes were *padlocked* to the rail.

ru: вызывать по громкой связи, вызывать на пейджер
gloss: To call someone over a loudspeaker or by sending a message to a pager or phone.
examples: *Page* the on-call doctor right away.
They *paged* him twice in the terminal.
The nurse is *paging* the surgeon now.

gloss: To make someone feel hurt or unhappy.
examples: It *pains* me to see the old theater torn down.
Her silence *pained* him more than the argument had.
He was visibly *pained* by the question.
contrast: As a verb *pain* is about feelings, and usually appears as *it pains me to*; for physical hurt Americans say *hurt*.

gloss: To lose color in the face, or to seem small and unimportant beside something else.
examples: Other problems *pale* beside this one.
She *paled* when the police car pulled into the driveway.
Last year's delays have *paled* next to this year's.
contrast: In the second sense it is nearly always *pale in comparison with* or *pale beside* something.

gloss: To criticize a film, book, or show very harshly in a review.
examples: Critics *pan* almost every sequel.
Reviewers *panned* the movie as loud and lazy.
The show was *panned* by everyone except its fans.
contrast: The n doubles: *panned*, *panning*. The same verb also means to swing a camera sideways (*the camera pans left*) and to wash gravel for gold (*pan for gold*).

gloss: To say or do whatever will please a group, even when it is cheap or dishonest.
examples: Candidates *pander* to whoever turns out to vote.
The network *pandered* to its loudest viewers.
He is *pandering*, and everyone in the room knows it.
contrast: Always with *to*: *pander to voters*.

gloss: To beg strangers for money in a public place.
examples: People *panhandle* at that freeway exit all day.
He *panhandled* outside the station for a week.
A man was *panhandling* by the bus stop.

ru: прыгать с парашютом; сбрасывать на парашюте
transitivity: both — transitive (*they parachuted supplies in*), intransitive (*he parachuted into the valley*)
gloss: To jump from an aircraft with a parachute, or to drop people or supplies by parachute.
examples: Smokejumpers *parachute* into fires no truck can reach.
The army *parachuted* food and blankets to the village.
She has *parachuted* from a plane twice.

gloss: To be very similar to something else, or to run alongside it.
examples: Her career *parallels* his almost exactly.
The new road *paralleled* the river for ten miles.
Sales are *paralleling* last year's numbers.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *paralleled*, *paralleling*; British writing doubles it.

gloss: To boil food briefly so that it finishes cooking some other way.
examples: *Parboil* the potatoes for five minutes before roasting them.
She *parboiled* the ribs to shorten the time on the grill.
The carrots are *parboiled*, then tossed in oil and salt.

ru: срезать, очищать от кожуры; урезать, сокращать
gloss: To cut the skin or outer layer off something, or to cut something down to a smaller size.
examples: *Pare* the apples before you slice them.
The company *pared* its staff by a third.
Costs have been *pared* to the bone.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *pair* and *pear*, which are different words.

gloss: To turn a small advantage into something much bigger.
examples: Athletes often *parlay* fame into a business.
She *parlayed* one viral video into a full-time job.
He is *parlaying* two terms on the city council into a run for governor.
contrast: Not the same as *parley*, which means to hold talks with an opponent.

gloss: To copy someone's style in an exaggerated way in order to make fun of it.
examples: Late-night shows *parody* whoever is in the news.
The sketch *parodied* the governor's accent.
His paintings have been *parodied* for decades.
contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: *parodies*, *parodied*, but *parodying* keeps the y.

gloss: To repeat someone else's words without understanding or thinking about them.
examples: Kids *parrot* whatever they hear at home.
The anchor simply *parroted* the press release.
He was *parroting* lines from a movie.
contrast: The t does not double, because the stress is on the first syllable: *parroted*, *parroting*.

gloss: To divide a country, a room, or a disk into separate parts.
examples: Folding screens *partition* the hall for small events.
Britain *partitioned* India in 1947.
The drive has been *partitioned* into two volumes.

gloss: To heat milk, juice, or another liquid enough to kill harmful bacteria.
examples: Dairies *pasteurize* milk before it is bottled.
They *pasteurized* the cider at a low temperature.
Most cheese sold here is made from *pasteurized* milk.
contrast: American spelling is *pasteurize*; British writing uses *pasteurise*.

gloss: To obtain an official right that stops others from making or selling your invention.
examples: Large firms *patent* thousands of small improvements a year.
He *patented* the design in 1974.
The process was *patented* by a lab in Ohio.

gloss: To sell goods from place to place, or to spread ideas that others think worthless or false.
examples: Vendors *peddle* umbrellas the moment it rains.
He *peddled* insurance door to door for years.
The site has been *peddling* conspiracy theories for months.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *pedal*, which means to push the pedals of a bicycle.

gloss: To urinate.
examples: The dog needs to *pee* before bed.
He *peed* in the bushes halfway up the trail.
The baby has been *peeing* through her diapers all week.
contrast: Informal but completely ordinary in speech and with doctors; in formal or medical writing use *urinate*.

gloss: To look quickly and secretly, especially through a small opening.
examples: Kids *peep* through the fence to watch practice.
She *peeped* around the corner to see who was there.
He was *peeping* through the blinds when the car pulled up.
contrast: *Peek* is a quick innocent look; *peep* often suggests spying, as in *Peeping Tom*.

gloss: To annoy someone in a small, nagging way.
examples: Little things *peeve* him more than big ones.
It *peeved* her that nobody said thank you.
He looked *peeved* when I mentioned the delay.

gloss: To fix a price, rate, or number at a set level, usually tied to something else.
examples: Several countries *peg* their currency to the dollar.
The board *pegged* the raise at three percent.
Rents are *pegged* to the cost-of-living index.
contrast: The g doubles: *pegged*, *pegging*. Informally, *peg someone as* means to size them up: *I pegged him as a lawyer*.

gloss: To write something such as a letter, an article, or a song.
examples: Columnists *pen* the same editorial every spring.
She *penned* the letter the night before she left.
The song was *penned* by a teenager.
contrast: The n doubles: *penned*, *penning*. Slightly literary; in ordinary speech people just say *write*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the bullet penetrated the wall*), intransitive (*the cold penetrated to the bone*)
gloss: To get into or through something, especially when that is hard to do.
examples: Sunlight barely *penetrates* the forest floor.
The blade *penetrated* two inches of oak.
Foreign firms have *penetrated* the market faster than anyone expected.

gloss: To hit or cover something with many small things, or to fill speech or writing with a lot of something.
examples: Reporters *pepper* the mayor with questions after every meeting.
Hail *peppered* the roof for twenty minutes.
His essay is *peppered* with quotations.

gloss: To make a hole or a line of small holes through something.
examples: Machines *perforate* the sheets so that they tear cleanly.
The ulcer *perforated* the wall of his stomach.
Stamps come *perforated* along the edges.

gloss: To curl hair chemically so that the curls last for months.
examples: Salons still *perm* hair, though the style comes and goes.
She *permed* her hair for the wedding.
His mother had her hair *permed* every spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the smell permeated the house*), intransitive (*water permeates through the soil*)
gloss: To spread through every part of something.
examples: Damp *permeates* the whole basement in spring.
The smell of smoke *permeated* every room in the house.
A quiet optimism was *permeating* the campaign.

gloss: To carry out something wrong, especially a crime or a hoax.
examples: Whoever *perpetrates* this kind of fraud rarely works alone.
They *perpetrated* a hoax that fooled three newspapers.
The attack was *perpetrated* by two men in a stolen car.
contrast: *Perpetrate* is to commit a crime; *perpetuate* is to keep something going, as in *perpetuate a myth*.

gloss: To be a perfect example of a quality, or to write about a thing as if it were a person.
examples: For many fans she *personifies* the whole team.
He *personified* everything the party wanted to show off.
Winter is often *personified* as an old man.
contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: *personifies*, *personified*, but *personifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To be connected with or relevant to something.
examples: These rules *pertain* only to full-time staff.
The judge read every document that *pertained* to the sale.
Questions *pertaining* to salary go to human resources.
contrast: Always with *to*. Formal: in speech people say *relate to* or *be about*.

gloss: To worry or unsettle someone.
examples: Loud noises *perturb* the horses.
The news *perturbed* him more than he let on.
She seemed *perturbed* by the question.

gloss: To read or look through something, either closely or, in looser modern use, casually.
examples: Take a minute to *peruse* the menu.
He *perused* the contract line by line.
She was *perusing* the shelves when I came in.
contrast: Traditionally *peruse* means to read very carefully; many Americans now use it for casual browsing, so the context decides.
